key_insight: The paper introduces a 3-D fracture-mitigation topology optimization method that uses dual topological derivatives both to create holes during design and to estimate crack-driving energy release rates from a single enriched finite element solve.
engineering_relevance: This enables designers of brittle solids to shape structures for lower fracture risk while avoiding repeated crack simulations, which can reduce computational cost in practical aerospace, civil, and mechanical design.
method: Level-set topology is parameterized with radial basis functions for shape evolution.
Interface-enriched finite elements capture the uncracked stress field accurately.
Dual topological derivatives estimate boundary energy release rates and guide hole nucleation; boundary ERRs are aggregated with a p-mean objective.
evidence_signal: The framework is demonstrated on 3-D numerical examples, including the standard L-bracket benchmark, showing its ability to mitigate fracture in brittle solids.
watch_item: Because the ERR estimates depend strongly on stress accuracy, the non-local stress-recovery and boundary enrichment strategy must be implemented carefully to avoid misleading crack-risk predictions.
paper_title: $\partial^2 ( \mathrm{TO} ) $: A Dual Topological Derivative-Based Enriched Topology Optimization for Fracture Mitigation in 3-D Brittle Solids
